newsitem.title: GERMANY: German tax row rumbles on ahead of debate.
newsitem.headline: German tax row rumbles on ahead of debate.

text.p: German politicians traded blame for the country's tax policy logjam on Monday ahead of a parliamentary debate which looked set to delay reforms indefinitely.

Commentators said the failure of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government to strike a compromise last week with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on much-needed tax reforms had badly damaged Bonn's standing in the eyes of the German public.
And an opinion poll showed that heavily-taxed Germans blamed the country's entire political class, rather than one side or the other, for the deadlock.

"The government and opposition have gambled away the last chance for a long time to prove they recognise the country's problems, and that they put the national good above their own power interests," news weekly Der Spiegel said.

"Nothing moves any more in Bonn. Unemployment is at record levels, state finances are out of control and the economic miracle of yesteryear has become a laughing stock. And the parties play at election campaigning," the magazine said.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plan to slash 30 billion marks ($16 billion) in income and corporate taxes was last week blocked by the opposition-controlled parliamentary mediation committee.

The committee formally rejected the package on Monday, deciding as expected only to abolish a capital trading tax on companies. The Bundestag lower house of parliament was to debate the rest of Waigel's tax reform package on Tuesday.

Kohl, who at the weekend accused the SPD of misusing its majority in the Bundesrat upper house in an "unscrupulous grab for power", wants to call a second round of parliamentary mediation to force the SPD into a climbdown on tax.

Peter Hintze, general secretary of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), told German Radio the government had "a small chance" of embarrassing the SPD into admitting it was blocking sound policies for purely tactical reasons.
The SPD accused the government of hypocrisy, and said that Kohl should call elections -- scheduled for September 1998 -- early to settle the tax issue.

"The government is selling a tax reform with revenue losses for the state which are irresponsibly high," finance spokesman Joachim Poss said, adding the Waigel tax reform would endanger German participation in European economic and monetary union.
"Even without this loss of revenues meeting the Maastricht criteria in this and future years is not certain," he said.
Bonn's tax deadlock comes just as a top economic think-tank said revenues could this year fall short even of the official forecasts made in May.
The Munich-based Ifo institute said revenues at federal and state level in the first half of the year, at 373 billion marks, were below half the 813 billion marks forecast for the full year.
"It appears that it will difficult to reach the tax targets of the official working group," Ifo wrote in a report.

Waigel said he expected Germany to qualify for EMU on the basis of the EMU criteria, but his budget arithmetic leaves no room for shortfalls without risking adherence to the budget deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product.
Worse, one of Germany's leading economists warned that if urgently-needed reforms to both the tax and pensions systems are postponed "revolutionary upheaval" could result.

"If a society no longer has the desire or the strength to pass necessary reforms by evolution, then one day the dam will break," Meinhard Miegel, head of the Bonn-based Institute for Economy and Society (IWG), told German Radio.
According to an opinion poll late last week, most Germans blame the government and opposition equally for the failure of the tax reform.

A survey by the Infratest polling group for ARD television found that 59 percent of Germans blamed both sides, 19 percent the government and just 12 percent the opposition for the collapse of the tax reforms. ($ = 1.863 German Marks)
